rows.explanation: It says all have left the way and become unprofitable, joining universal deviation to the loss-as-a-failed-account image.
It asks what benefit comes from gaining the whole world while losing oneself, directly casting ultimate loss as a failed transaction.
It measures worldly gain against the loss of one's own soul, matching the picture of self-loss in an account.
It asks what profit there is in gaining the world and losing one's soul, using the same profit-and-self-loss argument.
It declares that all have sinned and fall short of God's glory, a universal statement of deficit.
It says Scripture has shut up all under sin, portraying humankind as collectively enclosed in a ruinous condition.
It states that Jews and Gentiles alike are all under sin, closely matching the comprehensive judgment on humankind.
It puts both low and high people in the balance and finds them lighter than vanity, paralleling universal loss and weighing imagery.
It portrays people who think themselves rich yet do not know they are poor, blind, and naked, matching unsuspected loss beneath apparent gain.
It says all have gone astray like sheep, each turning to his own way, matching the universal lost-path reading.
It warns that a way seeming right to a person ends in death, matching self-deceived wandering that culminates in ruin.
It calls every man at his best state altogether vanity, a sweeping verdict of human futility despite apparent strength.
It asks what human can live without seeing death or deliver his soul from the grave, making self-loss through mortality universal.
It says all flesh would perish together and man return to dust, expressing a universal human undoing.
It says all have gone aside and none does good, a universal portrayal of people diverted from the right path.
It says death passed upon all people through sin, making universal mortality the outcome of humanity's condition.
It promises the believer no condemnation and passage from death to life, directly reversing a state of ultimate loss.
It says the Son will lose none entrusted to him but raise them at the last day, reversing final human loss.
It promises Christ's sheep eternal life and that they will never perish, the direct contrary of irreversible loss.
It promises that the believer will not perish but have everlasting life, stating the inverse final outcome.
It says God will redeem the psalmist's soul from the grave, directly answering the loss of self to death.
It promises that God will swallow up death in victory, reversing loss through death.
It declares all to be vanity, a sweeping wisdom verdict of futility akin to comprehensive loss.
It totals labor's result as vanity and no profit, reproducing the commercial reckoning of loss.
It says the whole world lies in wickedness, matching the image of humanity situated within an enveloping bad condition.
It says no living person can be justified before God, presenting a universal negative balance under judgment.
It describes its hearers' former state as dead in trespasses and sins, a condition rather than a passing setback.
It describes people as by nature children of wrath along with others, a condition of comprehensive exposure to judgment.
It says a wealthy person takes nothing at death, matching the loss of accumulated capital at the end.
It says an honored person who lacks understanding perishes like beasts, matching unrecognized loss beneath status.
It portrays days passing and years being spent away, closely matching time as a diminishing stake.
It says greed for gain takes away its owners' life, binding commercial gain to self-loss.
It says riches do not profit on the day of wrath while righteousness delivers from death, making final accounting decisive.
It asks what profit a person has from all labor under the sun, framing human work as a balance sheet.
It says one departs naked and takes nothing from labor, another image of a final negative balance.
It says a person's way is not in himself and that he cannot direct his own steps, matching loss as being off the right path.
It calls the heart deceitful and unknowable, matching the possibility of not seeing one's own ruin.
It finds a ruler weighed in balances and wanting, directly paralleling the deficient-scale image of loss.
It portrays Ephraim's strength being consumed without his knowing it, an image of unnoticed depletion.
It tells Israel that it has destroyed itself, directly expressing self-ruin even while naming God as help.
It depicts wages put into a bag with holes, a vivid image of capital steadily disappearing.
It says the broad way leads to destruction and many enter it, matching loss as the common course.
It says the narrow way leads to life and is found by few, providing the reverse outcome for an exceptional path.
It makes the rich man lose his life before he can possess his stored goods, exposing accumulation as a failed account.
It warns that unless people repent they will all perish, a universalized warning of ruin.
It says the desire to be rich sinks people into destruction and perdition, combining wealth pursuit with engulfing ruin.
It compares human life to a vapor appearing briefly and then vanishing, matching the time-limited dimension of loss.
It says turning a sinner from the error of his way saves a soul from death, directly answering lost-path self-destruction.
It says the world and its desire pass away while the doer of God's will abides, contrasting dissipating investment with enduring life.
It promises an order with no death, sorrow, crying, or pain, reversing final human ruin.
The sentence on Adam joins toilsome bread with return to dust, an archetypal scene of human undoing.
It says rejecters judge themselves unworthy of eternal life, a specific instance of self-incurred ultimate loss.
It asks what fruit came from shameful deeds and answers that their end is death, joining a profit calculation to ruin.
It calls death the wages of sin while contrasting God's gift of eternal life, using an account of ultimate loss and its reversal.
It makes sowing to the flesh reap corruption and sowing to the Spirit reap eternal life, treating conduct as an investment with ruin or life as its return.
It says one who seeks to save life loses it while one who loses it for Christ finds it, reversing ordinary self-loss through decisive exchange.
It says that saving one's life loses it while losing it for Christ and the gospel saves it, directly reversing self-loss.
It says that saving one's life loses it while losing it for Christ saves it, reversing the final outcome of loss.
It says loving one's life loses it while surrendering it in this world keeps it unto eternal life.
It depicts people claiming peace and safety when sudden destruction comes without escape, matching unsuspected loss beneath apparent security.
It calls man like vanity and his days a passing shadow, closely matching human life as vanishing capital.
It denies that anyone can give God a ransom to redeem a brother, matching ultimate personal loss beyond ordinary capital.
It calls treasure gained by deceit a vanishing vanity for seekers of death, binding commercial gain to ruin.
It promises ransom from the grave and redemption from death, directly reversing ultimate human loss.
It says finding one's life loses it while losing it for Christ finds it, making apparent self-preservation a losing exchange.
It says whoever seeks to save life loses it while whoever loses it preserves it, answering loss with its paradoxical reversal.
It warns that earthly treasure is corrupted or stolen, presenting accumulated capital as exposed to loss.
It commands treasure in heaven, where neither decay nor theft can destroy it, reversing the insecure-account image.
It warns unbelievers that they will die in their sins, portraying ruin as a condition in which they remain.
It says the Son of man came to seek and save what was lost, directly answering the condition of being lost.
It asks who could stand if God marked iniquities, presenting humanity as unable to survive a full divine reckoning.
It asks God to teach people to number their days so that they may gain wisdom, directly answering time as a spent resource.
The woman's argument compares inevitable death to water spilled beyond recovery, an image of irretrievable human loss.
It depicts a solitary laborer who never has enough riches and deprives his own soul of good, making accumulation self-bereaving.
It depicts someone with wealth and honor who cannot enjoy them because a stranger consumes them, making possession end in loss.
It says all flesh is grass and its glory withers like a flower, portraying universal human fading.
It says all have faded like a leaf and that their iniquities carry them away, combining universal failure with dispersal.
It has Israel describe its transgressions and sins as lying upon it while it pines away in them, closely matching an enclosing condition of loss.
In a divine oath, it calls the wicked to turn from their way and live rather than die, answering ruin with a way out.
It describes peoples laboring for fire and wearying themselves for vanity, an image of effort consumed without gain.
It says the outward person perishes while the inward person is renewed day by day, denying that visible decay is the believer's final loss.
It counts all things as loss in order to gain Christ, revaluing the entire ledger of gain and loss.
It says a person may suffer loss when work burns while the person is saved, explicitly separating lost work from a lost self.
It contrasts drawing back into perdition with believing unto the saving of the soul, setting preservation against final loss.
It says sin, when completed, brings forth death, tracing a course from inward desire to ruin.
It says all flesh is grass and its glory fades as a flower, reiterating universal human transience.
It says its hearers had been sheep going astray but have returned to the Shepherd of their souls, reversing lost wandering.
It says God does not will any to perish but calls all to repentance, opposing perishing with a way to life.
It warns believers to watch themselves so that they do not lose what they have worked for but receive a full reward.
It depicts those absent from the book of life being cast into the lake of fire, an ultimate judgmental loss.
